chief_complaint: numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that wakes her at night
hpi_details: A 68-year-old female presents to the clinic with numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that wakes her at night. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: thinks it might be carpal tunnel syndrome
concerns: She is worried that her hand will become too weak to safely hold and carry her new infant grandchild.
expectations: She hopes to be fitted with a wrist brace or given anti-inflammatory pills to stop her fingers from going numb at night.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Night splints, steroid injection, surgical release, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cervical radiculopathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Thenar wasting.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that wakes her at night. HPI: median nerve compression at flexor retinaculum.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Carpal Tunnel Syndrome.
reference_soap.plan: Begin with neutral-position night splinting and address contributing factors. Consider local corticosteroid injection for persistent symptoms. Refer for nerve-conduction studies or surgical release when there is thenar weakness/denervation, severe electrodiagnostic disease, or failure of conservative management.

teaching.one_liner: Median nerve compression at the wrist causing numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers that wakes the patient at night.

must_ask.say: Does this wake you up at night?
Do you do repetitive hand work?

history.answer: My right thumb, index, and middle fingers feel numb and tingly, and it's been waking me up in the middle of the night.
It is mostly a tingling and numb pins-and-needles sensation, though recently my hand feels slightly clumsy and weak.
It affects my right hand, specifically my thumb, index, and middle fingers, plus half of my ring finger. My pinky finger is completely fine.
The symptoms started about three weeks ago. It began fairly mildly, but it has been gradually getting worse.
At first it happened only once or twice a week, but lately it wakes me up almost every night and flares up during daytime tasks as well.
Yes, it wakes me from sleep around three or four in the morning with intense burning numbness and tingling in those three fingers.
When it wakes me, vigorously shaking my hand or dangling it off the edge of the bed helps ease the tingling after a few minutes.
Holding my phone for too long, gripping the steering wheel while driving, or cutting vegetables in the kitchen brings on the tingling right away.
I haven't had sudden paralysis, but my pinch grip feels a little weak when opening tight jar lids or turning keys.
I find myself accidentally dropping small cups or plates, and buttoning my cardigan takes longer because my fingertips feel clumsy.
No, I don't have any neck or back pain, and there is no sharp or shooting pain radiating down from my neck into my arm.
No slurred speech, no facial drooping, no blurry or double vision, and no dizziness at all.
No difficulty swallowing, no shortness of breath, no trouble chewing, and my eyelids do not droop.
My bowel and bladder habits are completely normal, and I don't have any numbness around my groin or buttocks.
I haven't noticed any muscle twitching, and the muscles in my hand look normal to me without shrinking.
No, I haven't had any cold, flu, diarrhea, or recent fever before this started.
I have been feeling quite fatigued and worn out during the day, mainly because the finger numbness keeps interrupting my sleep at night.
I spend a lot of time knitting blankets for my grandchildren, and I also do daily gardening and typing on my computer.
A neighbor had similar nighttime hand numbness and had carpal tunnel syndrome, so I've been wondering if that might be what I have.
I'm terrified that my grip is getting so weak that I might accidentally drop my new grandbaby.
I'm hoping you can give me a supportive wrist splint or something to take before bed so my hands stop waking me up.
I have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or high cholesterol.
I have never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, or health supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only have an occasional glass of wine at family dinners, maybe once or twice a month at most.
I eat a regular, balanced diet with plenty of meat and vegetables, and I've never had any stomach or bowel surgery.
I am a retired accountant living with my husband in an apartment, and I spend most of my days crafting and gardening.
No one in my family has a history of nerve disease, early stroke, or autoimmune disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, regular heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, body temperature 36.5°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and random capillary blood glucose 102 mg/dL.
Alert, well-nourished woman sitting comfortably, holding and lightly rubbing her right wrist, in no acute distress.
Facial symmetry intact with normal smile and eye closure; extraocular movements intact without ptosis or visual field deficits; speech is clear and fluent.
Shoulder, elbow, and wrist strength 5/5 bilaterally; right thumb abduction and opposition are 4+/5 with preserved thenar bulk and no visible atrophy; left hand strength is 5/5 throughout.

Decreased light touch and pinprick sensation over the palmar aspect of the right thumb, index, middle finger, and radial half of the ring finger; sensation over the hypothenar area, fifth digit, and left hand is fully intact.
Biceps, brachioradialis, triceps, patellar, and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric; bilateral Babinski responses are flexor.

Positive Phalen test reproducing tingling numbness in digits 1 to 3 within 30 seconds; positive Tinel sign with electric paresthesias radiating into the median nerve distribution on right volar wrist percussion; no wrist swelling or joint erythema.
Cervical spine has full active range of motion without midline tenderness; Spurling test is negative without radiating arm pain, and straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally.
No visible muscle fasciculations, twitches, involuntary movements, or resting tremor in any extremity.
Finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are smooth and intact bilaterally; tandem gait is steady and Romberg test is negative.
